A 59-year-old man presents to the emergency department with fatigue, worsening abdominal
discomfort, and progressive leg swelling over the past 3 months. He notes that the swelling is more
pronounced in the evenings. His only medication is ibuprofen for occasional joint pain. He does not
smoke and consumes 2–3 beers on weekends. Vital signs include a temperature of 36.0°C (96.8°F),
pulse of 82/min, respirations of 13/min, and blood pressure of 149/81 mm Hg. Pulmonary examination
reveals no abnormalities. Abdominal examination shows mild distension with shifting dullness, and the

liver is palpable 2–3 cm below the right costal margin. Applying pressure to the right upper quadrant
causes visible jugular vein distension lasting 15 seconds. The 2nd and 3rd metacarpophalangeal joints
of both hands are tender to palpation. There is 2+ edema in the lower extremities. What is the most
likely underlying cause of this patient's edema? Answer Choices: (A) Constrictive pericarditis (B)
Impaired hepatic albumin synthesis (C) Hyperdynamic circulation due to chronic anemia (D) Hepatic
venous outflow obstruction (E) Systemic inflammation with cytokine-mediated vascular permeability (F)
Macrovesicular steatosis of the liver (G) Impaired relaxation of the right ventricle (H) Increased capillary
hydrostatic pressure due to left ventricular failure (I) Chronic kidney disease with proteinuria (J) Portal
vein thrombosis
 A. Portal vein thrombosis
B. Constrictive pericarditis
C. Impaired relaxation of the right ventricle
D. Impaired hepatic albumin synthesis
E. Systemic inflammation with cytokine-mediated vascular permeability
F. Hepatic venous outflow obstruction
G. Hyperdynamic circulation due to chronic anemia
H. Chronic kidney disease with proteinuria
I. Macrovesicular steatosis of the liver
J. Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure due to left ventricular failure
